steps.action: The authors pose the aim: understand dispersion mechanisms and their relative dominance across spatial scales in a natural basin when celerity fields vary in space and time.
steps.quote: The objective of this study is to better understand the dispersion mechanisms taking place in a natural basin

steps.action: The authors adopt the DUC kinematic-wave spatially distributed travel time model, which they built and tested against hydrographs in the same basin in earlier work (Bunster et al. 2019a).
steps.quote: Using the same basin we consider, Bunster et al. (2019a) implemented and successfully tested the DUC method to predict the hydrograph at the basin outlet.

steps.action: They design the spatial analysis: DUC is run with every channel cell (area >2.5e5 m2) as a sub-basin outlet, and DG, DK and DKG are computed from Equations 1-3. Hydrodynamic dispersion is excluded.
steps.quote: the DUC method is executed for a homogeneously distributed runoff pulse for every cell in the basin

steps.action: They set the model conditions. These are the Quintero Creek basin and two sub-basins from a 30-m DEM, with roughness calibrated by Bunster et al. (2019a), and four uniform 5-min runoff pulses of 5, 10, 20 and 40 mm/hr.

end.claim: Within the Quintero Creek basin (about 0.25-90 km2), DG and DK increase with contributing area as power laws. Runoff intensity controls the hillslope-channel transition and so the relative contribution of DK and DG. DK's dependence on intensity inverts at about 8 km2, and DKG becomes intensity-independent above about 10 km2.

decisive_move.sentence: Computing spatially distributed, time-varying travel times with the DUC model for every cell treated as a sub-basin outlet is what produces the celerity and dispersion-coefficient fields on which every scaling claim rests.

gates.evidence: The model runs were set by a descriptive aim, not by a stated hypothesis. The results are compared with Di Lazzaro et al. (2016) theory (agreement only at 5 and 10 mm/hr) and with a constant-celerity baseline, but no observed data test the dispersion coefficients here. Intensities were chosen 'for simplicity and to allow comparison to previous studies' (p. 5); no analysis was fixed in advance.

imports.item: Kinematic wave theory and flood-wave celerity
Manning's equation for travel times on hillslopes and in channels
Single-direction flow algorithm for extracting drainage networks from DEMs (O'Callaghan & Mark 1984)
Pearson correlation between channel and hillslope lengths used in the Di Lazzaro et al. scaling theory

novelty_claims.quote: Nevertheless, an explicit and distributed dynamic representation of the travel times has not been used for this purpose.
For this purpose, and in contrast with previous approaches, we explicitly consider individual flow paths and local conditions

limits: The paper is purely model-based. Travel times are not checked against observations here; the hydrograph validation and the roughness calibration are inherited from Bunster et al. (2019a). Only one basin is studied, and the two 'independent' sub-basins are nested parts of it, so the generalization is weak. The authors say the 8 km2 and 10 km2 thresholds must be tested elsewhere. Fitted power laws carry no uncertainty or goodness-of-fit statistics. The roughness sensitivity is run only at 10 mm/hr. Runoff pulses are uniform, so spatial variability of runoff production is not addressed. Hydrodynamic dispersion is excluded by construction. No review file was supplied, so the review history is unknown. Composition is none_fits (inference): this is a simulation-based scaling analysis with model-set conditions and no rival test, which matches none of the listed walks. Sub-claim statuses: celerity scaling (channel celerity as a power law, hillslope celerity roughly constant) is regularity_in_range. DK intensity inversion at ~8 km2 is regularity_in_range, for this basin only. The basin-size nonlinearity hypothesis is none (untested). The constant-celerity bias of DG (crossover at ~2 km2) is regularity_in_range. Roughness effects are regularity_in_range, at 10 mm/hr only.

disagreements.quote: Such significant differences illustrate the importance of considering a fully distributed celerity field when calculating

disagreements.support: The modeled celerity ratio varies considerably with sub-basin scale and runoff intensity (Figure 2d), and differs between the sub-basins.
disagreements.quote: Hence, using a constant ratio of celerities in channel and hillslopes to calculate the dispersion coefficients might not capture the effects at the sub-basin scale.

disagreements.quote: which is in agreement with our results for runoff intensities of 5 and 10 mm/hr
